topic: NVIDIA-Certified Professional: Generative AI and LLMs (NCP-GENL) exam preparation - NVIDIA's professional certification for designing, fine-tuning, optimizing, deploying, and evaluating large language models with distributed training and the NVIDIA software stack
cert_name: NVIDIA-Certified Professional: Generative AI and LLMs
exam_format: 60-70 questions, 120 minutes, online proctored remotely (registration via a Certiverse account). NCP-GENL is a professional-tier credential. NVIDIA does not publicly publish the passing score or official per-domain percentage weightings, so the domain weights in this course are editorial estimates that reflect the published objective emphasis, not NVIDIA's official figures.
question_types: multiple choice (single answer, exactly 4 options) and multiple response clearly marked as 'Select TWO/THREE'
audience: ML engineers, applied scientists, and LLM developers who design, train, fine-tune, optimize, and deploy large language models. Candidates should have 1-2 years of hands-on deep-learning and LLM experience plus Python and GPU/PyTorch familiarity. A professional step up from the NVIDIA NCA-GENL (Generative AI Associate) and a companion to the NVIDIA NCP-AAI, NCP-AIO, and NCA-AIIO courses in this catalog.
author: Aseem Mankotia

domains.name: LLM Foundations and Architecture
domains.notes: Transformer internals at professional depth: self-attention and multi-head attention, positional encodings, encoder/decoder vs decoder-only, and modern efficiency variants (FlashAttention, grouped-query attention, mixture-of-experts). Model families and scaling laws, context-window mechanics and extension, and tokenization (BPE, SentencePiece) and its effects. Understanding why an architecture choice affects quality, cost, and latency for a described workload.

domains.name: Prompt Engineering and Adaptation
domains.notes: Advanced prompting and in-context learning: zero/one/few-shot, chain-of-thought and self-consistency, ReAct and tool-augmented prompting, structured output and constrained decoding. Retrieval-augmented generation as an adaptation strategy. The key decision the exam tests: when to prompt, when to use RAG, and when to fine-tune, given accuracy, cost, data, and latency constraints. Prompt evaluation and iteration.

domains.name: Data Preparation and Fine-Tuning
domains.notes: Dataset curation, cleaning, deduplication, and tokenization for training; instruction-tuning data design. Customization strategies and their trade-offs: full fine-tuning vs parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA/QLoRA, adapters, P-tuning), continued pretraining/domain adaptation, and preference optimization (RLHF, DPO). Customizing with NVIDIA NeMo. Choosing the right customization technique for a described data budget and objective.

domains.name: Optimization and Acceleration
domains.notes: The heaviest domain and the NVIDIA hardware angle. Distributed training strategies: data, tensor, pipeline, and sequence parallelism, ZeRO/sharding, and gradient checkpointing. Mixed precision (FP16/BF16/FP8), memory and batch optimization, and throughput tuning across multi-GPU/multi-node. Inference acceleration with TensorRT-LLM, quantization (INT8/FP8/AWQ/GPTQ), KV-cache management, continuous/in-flight batching, and speculative decoding. Selecting the optimization that meets a described performance/cost target.

domains.name: Deployment, Serving, and Monitoring
domains.notes: Building scalable inference pipelines on the NVIDIA stack: NVIDIA NIM microservices, Triton Inference Server, model repositories, and containerized orchestration (Kubernetes). Autoscaling, load balancing, and multi-model/multi-tenant serving; latency vs throughput vs cost trade-offs. Real-time monitoring, reliability, canary/blue-green rollouts, and lifecycle/MLOps for LLMs (versioning, retraining triggers, drift). Choosing the right serving and scaling pattern for an SLA.

domains.name: Evaluation and Responsible AI
domains.notes: Evaluating LLMs: benchmarks and task metrics, LLM-as-judge, human evaluation, and error/failure analysis. Detecting and mitigating hallucination, bias, and toxicity; guardrails with NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails; safety, compliance, privacy, and data governance. Responsible-AI practices across the model lifecycle. Choosing the correct evaluation method or guardrail for a described quality or safety requirement.

extra_guidance: NCP-GENL is NVIDIA's professional Generative AI and LLMs certification - the technical, hardware-forward step up from the popular NCA-GENL associate cert already in the catalog, and it completes the NVIDIA professional track with NCP-AAI (this batch) and NCP-AIO. The differentiator vs the associate exam is DEPTH: distributed training, GPU/inference optimization, and production serving on the NVIDIA stack. CRITICAL accuracy note: NVIDIA does NOT publish official per-domain percentage weightings or the passing score for NCP-GENL, so present the domain NAMES as the exam's objective areas but mark the weights as editorial estimates (leading '~'), never as NVIDIA's official figures - state this where weights appear. This is a decision-and-optimization exam: the skill is choosing the right adaptation, parallelism, quantization, or serving strategy for a described accuracy/cost/latency constraint, so practice questions MUST be scenario-based with plausible distractors and 'BEST / MOST memory-efficient / HIGHEST throughput' framing. Cover the classic decision pairs relentlessly: prompt vs RAG vs fine-tune, full fine-tuning vs LoRA/QLoRA, RLHF vs DPO, data vs tensor vs pipeline parallelism, FP16 vs BF16 vs FP8, INT8 vs FP8 vs AWQ/GPTQ quantization, TensorRT-LLM vs vanilla inference, NIM vs custom Triton serving. Anchor everything to the NVIDIA software stack (NeMo, NIM, TensorRT-LLM, Triton, NeMo Guardrails, Megatron) - that is the vendor angle and a frequent source of exam questions. Labs are NVIDIA-tooling walkthroughs at read-and-understand depth (LoRA fine-tune in NeMo, quantize with TensorRT-LLM, serve with NIM/Triton, add NeMo Guardrails), not deep CUDA kernel work. Final chapter must be a full exam simulation with a 120-minute time-management strategy for 60-70 questions and guidance on multiple-response elimination. Scan the practice bank for other-vendor terms (AWS/Azure/GCP) before upload per the pipeline compliance rules.
